utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Today is Monday, the 7th of March, 2012 -- 5th of March, 2012. I would like to greet all the people present in the courtroom, Mr. Marcussen and his associates, Mr. Seselj, as well as all the people assisting us in this courtroom. I must apologise, we are running slightly late for a reason which was out of my control. In the decision we issued a while ago, we specified that the Prosecution would have ten hours for its closing arguments and the Defence - represented by Mr. Seselj - will also have ten hours. So in this week we shall address the closing arguments of the Prosecution and during the second week we will address the closing arguments of the Defence. That said, Mr. Marcussen, I shall now give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Your Honours, before I start, I would like to inform the Trial Chamber that the -- for the Prosecution, the counsel who will be appearing will be, in addition to myself, Ms. Biersay, who's with me here today. We will also have Mr. Mussemeyer, Ms. Hochhauser, Ms. Iodice, and Mr. Traldi. We're not having the full Prosecution team in court for logistical reasons, so counsel will be appearing as they are required to make their arguments. I will also inform the Chamber that the Prosecution will not be needing ten hours for its arguments.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, I believe that five representatives of the OTP who would be presenting closing arguments are too few. I think that at least one should handle each hour of their arguments because they're unable to speak reasonably for -- and make sense for longer than one hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The closing arguments of the Prosecution are conducted in a way in which the Prosecution wishes. Please proceed, Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Your Honours, exactly 20 years ago today, on the 5th of March, 1992, the accused vowed that the Serbian Radical Party was ready to oppose with all means available Bosnia and Herzegovina from becoming independent. He threatened that if it declared independence there would be "rivers of blood on Bosnia and Herzegovina's soil." That is from Exhibit P1324. The day after the accused's threat, Bosnia and Herzegovina declared independence. By the end of March 20 years ago, rivers of blood flowed in Bosnia and Herzegovina the same way they had flowed in Croatia after it had declared independence. The accused's threat of rivers of blood became brutal reality for Witness VS-1064. VS-1064 was 22 years old. He was born and lived in Kostjerevo, Zvornik. No one had ever looked at him differently because he was a Muslim until the war broke out in Croatia, and Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina started to prepare for war. In April 1992, Serb forces attacked and cleansed Zvornik town of its non-Serb population. Only a few non-Serb villages within the municipality still remained to be cleansed. One of them was Kostjerevo. The inhabitants from the village were promised that nothing would happen to them. So when the JNA ordered them to surrender their hunting weapons, they did so. But on the 30th of May, 1992, the army attacked their village. They did not fight back. Nonetheless, the inhabitants were forced out of their homes and the men were separated from the women and children. The women and children were expelled to Muslim-held areas. VS-1064 was alone there with his father and his three brothers. One of them was only 17 years old. Serb TO forces detained them and the other men in the Drinjaca Dom Kulture. The prisoners were given no food, no water. The guards humiliated them. They forced them to make the Serb Orthodox three-finger salute to be allowed to use the bathroom, but humiliation was nothing compared to what was to come. Soon, a group of Arkan's men stormed into the Dom Kulture. They forced the prisoners to sing Chetnik songs and to insult them they called them Balija and Ustasha. They beat them. VS-1064, his father and brother, all the men were beaten by Arkan's men. They beat the prisoners with batons and stabbed them. They beat the prisoners with batons and stabbed them. They beat the prisoners so badly that one of them begged: "Give me a rifle to kill myself. I can't take it anymore." After stabbing one of the prisoners, the leader of the group, with the bloody knife still in his hand, threatened: "You will see what the Chetniks are this evening." Then Arkan's men left. In the evening, a group of Seseljevci arrived. VS-1064 recalled that he was so scared that he did not dare to look at them, fearing that if their eyes met they would harm him. They started to select detainees and took them out in small groups. After each group was taken out, VS-1064 heard gun-fire. The men were taken out but they did not come back. The Seseljevci did come back. Then it was VS-1064's turn. He was taken out with other men from his village. The Seseljevci started shooting. VS-1064 fell to the ground wounded. The shooting stopped and the Seseljevci started to celebrate, firing into the air. As soon as they left back inside, VS-1064 managed to get up and run away. He saw a small group of people lying on the concrete nearby. They were all dead, all dead except for one who was calling out for his mother. After the war, the victims of the massacre were exhumed. VS-1064 identified the remains of his father and three brothers amongst the 88 corpses. This case is about the accused's responsibility for the crimes committed against VS-1064 and all the other victims of the crimes in Vukovar, Zvornik, Greater Sarajevo, Mostar, Nevesinje, and Hrtkovci that have been proven in this case. The evidence proves beyond a reasonable doubt that the crimes set out in the indictment have been established. Specifically, tens of thousands of innocent non-Serb civilians, primarily Croats and Muslims, were forcibly transferred and deported. Croats and Muslims who were not expelled were detained under inhumane conditions. They were beaten, tortured raped, or submitted to other sexual violence. 905 persons were killed, most in organised massacres or in detention facilities. Croat and Muslim property was looted and wantonly destroyed, and religious sites were destroyed and desecrated. Croat and Muslims were persecuted through acts such as dismissals from their work, deprivation of pensions, and measures to prevent them from returning to their homes after they had been expelled. The accused physically committed crimes in Vukovar and Hrtkovci, and he is responsible for crimes carried out by Serb forces, including Seseljevci, during the persecutorial campaign in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina as a member of a joint criminal enterprise. The evidence also proves that the accused instigated and aided and abetted the perpetrators of the crimes charged in the indictment. The Prosecution's closing arguments will address the following issues: First, we will show that the accused was a member of a joint criminal enterprise to commit the crimes charged in the indictment. I will be presenting the Prosecution's argument about the existence of the joint criminal enterprise. Ms. Biersay will address the accused's contribution to the joint criminal enterprise and to the crimes by inciting the crimes and aiding and abetting the perpetrators of the crimes. Second, we will address the crimes charged in the indictment. Ms. Hochhauser will cover Vukovar. Mr. Mussemeyer will deal with evidence relating to so-called pattern municipalities in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. Ms. Iodice will address Your Honours regarding Zvornik and Greater Sarajevo. Mr. Traldi will cover two municipalities as well: Mostar and Nevesinje. And Ms. Biersay will deal with the accused's crimes in Hrtkovci. Finally, I will conclude and present the Prosecution's arguments on sentencing. So I turn now to the Prosecution's argument regarding the JCE alleged in the indictment. Your Honours, the evidence proves beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused participated in the preparation and execution of a joint criminal enterprise; its common purpose was to forcibly create ethnically-separate territories in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. Its common purpose was implemented from at least August 1991, when Serb forces engaged in a massive persecutorial campaign against non-Serbs, mainly Croats and Muslims, in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. The crimes in Vukovar, Zvornik, Greater Sarajevo, Mostar, and Nevesinje were part of this persecutorial campaign. They were committed by Serb forces under the command of or controlled by members of the joint criminal enterprise. Many of the most savage crimes were committed by Serb volunteers recruited, organised, and deployed by the accused. His volunteers were notorious for their brutality and crimes, and his volunteers were so closely associated with him that they were commonly known as Seseljevci - Seselj's men. Seseljevci participated in and committed crimes in all the crime-base municipalities charged in the indictment. JNA forces also participated in and committed crimes which have been proven in this case. JCE member Slobodan Milosevic, the president of the Republic of Serbia, controlled the JNA. JCE members and JNA Generals Veljko Kadijevic and Blagoje Adzic were the most senior officers in the JNA. Members of the special operation unit of the Serbian MUP, known as the Red Berets, were also participants in and perpetrators of crimes. Milosevic also controlled the Serbian MUP and worked closely with JCE members Jovica Stanisic, chief of the State Security Service of the Serbian MUP; and his deputy, Franko Simatovic, also known as Frenki. And the Serbian MUP co-operated closely with JCE member Zeljko Raznatovic, known as Arkan. He controlled a paramilitary organisation called Arkan's men or Arkan's Tigers, who also participated in and perpetrated crimes in the indictment. In Croatia, members of local Serb police and Territorial Defence forces participated in crimes. They were under the control of JCE members Goran Hadzic, prime minister of the SAO of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, president of the government of the same SAO, and later president of the RSK, the Republic of Serbian Krajina; JCE member Radovan Stojicic, also known as Badza, was a MUP commander in the SAO of SBWS in 1991. In Bosnia and Herzegovina, members of local Serb police forces and Territorial Defence forces as well as members of the Army of Republika Srpska, the VRS, perpetrated and participated in crimes. They were under the command or control of JCE member Radovan Karadzic, the president of the SDS in Bosnia and Herzegovina and from the 12th of May, 1992, president of the Presidency of the Republika Srpska, the RS; JCE member Biljana Plavsic was a member of the RS Presidency; JCE member Momcilo Krajisnik, the president and speaker of the Serb Assembly of the RS also had control over these forces; and finally JCE member Ratko Mladic was the commander of the Main Staff of the VRS. The participation of all these forces in the crimes charged in the indictment was the result of close co-operation between these JCE members as well as others, such as JCE member Radmilo Bogdanovic, who facilitated the arming of Serbs in both Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. The crimes were committed by these forces because the accused and other JCE members were united by a common goal: The creation of a Serb state, as I will now discuss. Uniting Serbs in one Greater Serbia was a vision that the accused had long nurtured and it was a pillar of his political programme. As part of his political platform, the accused revived the Chetnik ideology and militaristic traditions from the First and Second World Wars. The Chetnik Movement's core goal boiled down to a struggle for territorial control over Greater Serbia and the expulsion of non-Serbs from targeted areas to ensure Serb dominance. To publicise and advance his goal of a Greater Serbia, the accused published "Velika Srbija," which means "Greater Serbia." On the cover of the first issue of Velika Srbija was a map of Greater Serbia. It is in evidence as Exhibit P38. Exhibit P26, which should now be shown on the screen, shows the accused's vision of his Greater Serbia. It includes present-day Serbia, Macedonia, Montenegro, Kosovo, Bosnia and Herzegovina, as well as much of Croatia. As he said in Exhibit P1175, the accused wanted to amputate Croatia at what he claimed to be the old Serbian border running between the towns of Karlobag, Ogulin, Karlovac, and Virovitica, the KOKV line. If Your Honours look at the upper left part -- we seem to be having some technical issues. If I may turn Your Honours attention back to the map. If Your Honours look at the upper left part of the map on your screen, the KO KV line is a border between the areas shaded in red and the area shaded in brown. The accused also engaged in a vicious and relentless propaganda campaign against non-Serbs, including Croatians and Muslims as well as Kosovar Albanians. He claimed that Serbs had an historic right to the territory of Greater Serbia. He denigrated and dehumanised non-Serbs. He equated Croatians to Ustasha fascists who had committed crimes against Serbs and Bosnian Muslims to Ottoman Turks that he said had subjugated Serbs for hundreds of years. He claimed that Serbs were under an imminent threat of genocide at the hands of Croats and the enslavement by Muslims. He repeatedly raised the spectre of crimes against Serbs during the Second World War and he called for blind revenge in which rivers of blood would flow. Today the accused's message is clear. Two decades ago, against the backdrop of increased violence, escalating tension, and ultimately war that tore the former Yugoslavia apart, the accused's message was even clearer. He called for crimes to be committed against Croats and Muslims so his Chetnik vision of a Greater Serbia could be realised. The accused also revived the Chetnik militaristic organisation under the umbrella of his political activities. In 1989, he received the Chetnik military title traditionally bestowed on Chetnik leaders, Vojvoda, from Second World War Chetnik leader Momcilo Djujic. The accused established the Serbian Chetnik Movement which we will refer to with the acronym SCP. In 1991 the accused incorporated the SCP into his new party, the Serbian Radical Party, the SRS. The SCP became the military wing of the SRS. He then created a Crisis Staff, and later turned it into a War Staff, through which he recruited and deployed his volunteers, the Seseljevci. His military persona extended to the front lines where he wore military uniform and visited his Seseljevci. Your Honours now have on the screen before you Exhibit P184. You see the accused in uniform, wearing a helmet, and he's surrounded by other people in uniform. And on the helmet of the accused you see a white eagle. This white eagle is a tradition Serb symbol. The accused has at times challenged witnesses who associated Seseljevci with the white eagle symbols because there existed another paramilitary formation with the name White Eagles. This picture shows that the symbol was also used by the SRS. Indeed, as the accused explained in Exhibit P184 -- excuse me, Exhibit P185 at page 1 , his Seseljevci scratched the communist symbol of the five-pointed star off of army helmets and drew white eagles in their place. I will refer Your Honours' attention to the person to the left of the accused in the front of the picture who wears a cap. At transcript page 6046, Witness VS-007 identified this person as Milan Lancuzanin, also known as Kameni, who led the Seseljevci in Vukovar and was one of the key perpetrators of the massacre at Ovcara. This evidence clearly shows that the accused was ready to pursue his Greater Serbia by all means available as he said 20 years ago. And soon he would be able to do so. When communism lost its legitimacy in the late 1980s, nationalists in the republics that formed the former Yugoslavia began to seek independence, first in Slovenia and Croatia and soon also in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Many Serb leaders opposed this prospect. They were especially determined to prevent independence of the republics of Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina because it would separate Serbs by international borders and leave sizeable groups of Serbs as minorities in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. To avoid separating Serbs in different states, they sought to turn much of Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina into Serb-dominated territory. These efforts manifested themselves in the creation of Serb Autonomous Regions, or SAOs, in Croatia and later in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The efforts were supported by Milosevic, who had risen to power on a Serb nationalist agenda and was seen as a protector and patron of Serbs outside the Republic of Serbia, as noted by the Trial Chamber in its adjudicated fact decision of 10th of December, 2007, facts number 48 to 50. I will in the following be referring to this decision as AF-1. The accused and Milosevic recognised their common nationalist agenda and set aside their political differences. The accused explained during the indictment period: "It is not important how Milosevic's regime treated me in the past, what's most important is how he handles Serb national interests today." That is from Exhibit P1215, page 8. They pursued this common goal by establishing Serb Autonomous Regions and Serb military forces which fought for the control of those regions. The creation of the SAOs formalised the Serb nationalist territorial aspirations by declaring parts of Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina to be Serb land. They were the first step towards an all-Serb nation. Your Honours have in front of you now on the screen a map which shows the different SAOs that were declared and the way they looked before the war broke out. Leaders of the Serbian Democratic Party, or the SDS, in Croatia declared SAOs in three targeted areas: In Krajina, in Western Slavonia, in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. Leaders of these SAOs included JCE members Milan Babic and Goran Hadzic. Milan Babic was the president of the SAO of Krajina, which Your Honours can see is the big turquoise area to the left which is now being indicated on the screen. And Goran Hadzic was the president of the SAO of SBWS, which is on the opposite side over here, which is now being indicated. In Bosnia, the coloured areas represent the different SAOs that were declared there. JCE member Radovan Karadzic, the president of the SDS in Bosnia and Herzegovina, explained the objective of these SAOs. He declared that if Bosnia and Herzegovina left Yugoslavia "the only option ... is Greater Serbia." That is in Exhibit P877, paragraph 97 -- sorry, paragraph 39. Karadzic repeated his call for Greater Serbia in February 1992 in Exhibit P503. And the accused recognised that the SDS had the same goal of creating a single Serb state. That can be seen, for instance, in Exhibit P1248 at page 4 [sic]. I will now indicate on the same map, Your Honours, where the crime-base locations in this indictment are found as well as the so-called pattern municipalities. The red dots indicate the crime-base areas in the indictment. So Vukovar is situated in the SBWS close to the border with Serbia on the River Drina -- no, that's incorrect. I apologise. Down in Bosnia, Zvornik is situated close to the border with Serbia on the Drina River. As Your Honours can see on this map, this is in a grey area indicated on the map, which means that it was not initially part of the SAOs. Also, the area around Sarajevo where crimes were committed is in a grey area which was not part of the SAOs yet. And Mostar, similarly, was not part of the SAOs. But together with Nevesinje, Brcko, and Bijeljina and Bosanski Samac, all these locations were in strategic, important places, and therefore when the war broke out in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Serb forces took these areas and expelled non-Serbs from them. This evidence proves that the accused and other Serb leaders in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina shared the common purpose of creating a Serb-dominated territory in these targeted areas and beyond. Because of their aspiration for a Serbian state, the accused supported Serb leaders in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. The accused established his Serbian Radical Party in February 1991 and committed the party to support the SDS. That can be seen in Exhibit P153 at page 13, where he specifically mentions that the SRS is willing to support the SDS in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, and so he did. In March 1991, for example, the accused travelled to Krajina to lend support to JCE member Babic and call for a Serbian Krajina where "there is no room for Ustashas." That is from Exhibit P335 at page 1. In the SBWS he held rallies and met with local Serb leaders to discuss organising Serb military forces in the area. He then deployed Seseljevci to, for example, Borovo Selo at their request. That can be seen in Exhibits P55 and P2 -- sorry, P1277, and the testimony of Witness VS-004. In Bosnia and Herzegovina, the accused met with JCE member Karadzic to discuss the taking over of targeted areas, and he lauded Karadzic in his speeches. That can be seen in Exhibits P1003, P1339, P1176, and others. He later described their meetings, saying: "We knew then that it would come" -- my apologies, Your Honours. "We knew then that it would come to a conflict, to a war. In any case, I had already met with my Chetniks there. We had a detailed map of the eastern part of Bosnia in front of us and we were considering actions for a take-over of Visegrad, Visegrad bridge, Zvornik, et cetera. At that time it was obvious that there was going to be war." And that is from Exhibit P1246 at page 3. Serb leaders in Croatia sought military assistance from the accused. In Exhibit P31, the accused admitted that he sent Seseljevci to the SAO Krajina at the request of JCE member Babic. From 1991 to 1992, JCE members Hadzic and Martic travelled to the SRS War Staff office in Belgrade to request volunteers. This is in Exhibit P1074 at paragraph 46. Local TO leaders also requested the -- I believe I said page 46 and I should have said paragraph 46 -- 86. Local TO leaders also requested that the accused deploy Seseljevci to support their forces. In the crime bases and pattern municipalities in Croatia, the accused responded directly to such requests. When the Vukovar TO sent the SRS War Staff a request for Seseljevci, the accused decided that the SRS should send "as many volunteers as possible." That is in Exhibit C-11 at page 14. Seseljevci were deployed to Western Slavonia - where Vocin, one of our pattern municipalities, is located - upon the request of local TO forces. That is in the testimony of VS-004 and VS-033 and in Exhibit P223. Many other local leaders in Croatia also requested fighters from the accused. This can be seen, for instance, in Exhibits P942, in relation to Sisak; P264, in relation to Okucani; P239, in relation to Novska; and P226, Podravska Slatina. And these deployments of Seseljevci were supported by the Serbian MUP. The accused co-operated with the Serbian MUP through Witness Petkovic, as he stated in Exhibit P644 at page 9. Petkovic described this co-operation in his evidence. He had numerous meetings with JCE member Stanisic and JCE member Simatovic, as Witness Stefanovic confirms. Through the MUP, Seseljevci were later deployed to Vukovar, received training at a centre in Lipovaca, outside Sid in Serbia, which was organised by the Serbian MUP. This can be seen in Witness Rankic's evidence. And JCE member Arkan, who was affiliated with the State Security Service of the MUP of Serbia, provided logistical support to Seseljevci at his base in Erdut in Eastern Slavonia. The accused personally brought Seseljevci to Erdut and addressed the volunteers, telling them that: "Ustashas should be killed and expelled." This is in Exhibit P528, paragraph 32; and also in supporting evidence found in Exhibits P921, at page 2; P1257, at page 30; and in evidence by Witness Rankic, found in Exhibit P1074, at paragraphs 85 and 86. Milosevic also provided large-scale assistance to local Serb forces. Through his trusted men in the Serbian MUP, JCE members Stanisic, Simatovic, and Bogdanovic, Milosevic provided military support to Serb leaders in Krajina and local police forces were trained and armed. They promised JCE member Babic 20.000 guns. In the SAO SBWS, Milosevic and Bogdanovic gave the local Serb TO weapons. Those weapons were passed on to Seseljevci who had been deployed to the SBWS, evidencing the close support between JCE members in Belgrade, locally in various areas in Croatia, and the accused. This evidence is found in Exhibits P1137, at pages 115 to -16; and in Exhibit P1252 at page 3; and in Exhibit P644. The Serbian MUP also participated in acts of provocation to engage Croat forces in conflict. After the conflicts erupted, the JNA would enter supposedly to calm the situation. In reality, once the clash was over, the JNA would secure Serb territorial gains. This is found again in Exhibit P1137, at page 92 and to page 94; in Exhibit P1 -- oh, I thought there was a comment. I'm sorry. In Exhibit P412, pages 1 to 4; and in transcript page 3968, which is expert witness Theunens' testimony. From the second half of 1991, the Republic of Serbia intensified its practical assistance to Croatia in the form of weapons, communication equipment, and other supplies to Serbs in Croatia. It also reveals that the Republic of Serbia was financing the salaries and pension contribution of approximately 50.000 Serb TO members throughout the SAO Krajina, SAO Western Slavonia, and the SAO of SBWS. This is found in Exhibit P932. Moreover, the Serbian MUP also created its own special police unit - that I've mentioned before - to carry out the common purpose of the JCE members, known to many as the Red Berets. In Exhibit P131, which is a video, Stanisic, Slobodan Milosevic, and Simatovic are seen proudly discussing their accomplishments during the war. In this unique video, which we will be showing in a moment, these key JCE members celebrate their common accomplishments in pursuit of the persecutorial campaign in Croatia and in Bosnia. Your Honours will see Simatovic explains that the Red Berets were deployed extensively throughout Croatia and Bosnia, as he says, throughout the entire Serb ethnic area. And he'll also explain that the unit was created in May of 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't hear a thing. As I've told you, Your Honours, there is a lot of material to present and too few people from the Prosecution. They're just not capable of pulling this off as they should. How many mistakes they've already made.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are waiting for the technical problem to be resolved, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we are waiting, Your Honours, are you not ashamed to see that there are five people appearing on behalf of the Prosecution and I am on my own. On behalf of Defence, it is just me. It seems that this is something you find okay, that you like it, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I propose we continue without seeing the video. That can be reviewed by the Chamber at its leisure during deliberation. I would note that in this video, Stanisic describes the extensive operations of the Red Berets. He explained, for example, that the unit had operations in 50 locations, they had 26 training centres for local Serb forces, and they included training centres in areas of particular interest to this case, namely Vukovar, Bijeljina, Bosanski Samac, Brcko, and Trebinje, that Your Honours will be hearing more about during the Prosecution's arguments. It also explains that the unit set up and operated a network of airfields. This reward ceremony took place at a location which was named after what was described as a distinguished member of the unit, Radoslav Kostic. And Your Honours will be hearing more about him and his involvement in arming of local Serbs, both in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina and notably in the Zvornik area, later on in the Prosecution's submissions. Now, the accused not only provided support to the local TOs in Croatia during this period and co-operated with the Serbian MUP. The accused also provided significant support to the JNA. Their co-ordinated efforts to train, arm, and deploy Seseljevci are discussed in paragraphs 100 to 106 of the Prosecution's closing brief. As the conflict in Croatia developed, the JNA became a Serb army under Milosevic's control. By the summer of 1991, the JNA leadership accepted Milosevic's directions "without any discussion." This is found in Exhibit P198 at page 6. And it adopted a new nationalist goal. As JCE member Kadijevic stated in his book about the breakup of the former Yugoslavia, this new mission of the JNA became: "... to protect the Serb people" -- Your Honours, I believe we now have the audio on but -- at least I have it in my headphone, so I propose we don't need it. Yeah, I think there are no --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I could help them with the technical problem if they can't do it because I'm very well-versed in all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mentioned General Kadijevic's book. What is the number of the document, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: That is Exhibit P196 and I will now quote from page 73 of that exhibit. At that place, General Kadijevic explains what the new mission of the JNA had become. It had become: "To protect the Serb people in Croatia in such a way that all regions with a majority Serb population would be completely free from the presence of the Croatian Army and the Croatian authorities." The accused approved of the JNA's new goal. He explained: "JNA is also Serbian, for it is our only army, and events have shown that the JNA too has only us. Therein, the JNA is ours." That is in Exhibit P1281 at page 3. However, the JNA faced a manpower shortage due to desertions and its own efforts to purge non-Serbs from its ranks. To fill the manpower gap, its leadership turned to the accused. As he testified --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One minute, please. May I ask the French booth to be in line with what Mr. Marcussen is saying. It's difficult to hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Would Your Honours like me to go back to the quote that I read out or ...?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, for those who listen to you. Yes, please, could you repeat the quote.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So what I was saying was that the accused approved of the new goal of the JNA, and he said: "The JNA is also Serbian, for it is our only army, and events have shown that the JNA too has only us. Therein, the JNA is ours." Exhibit P1281 at page 3. And I continue from here. However, the JNA faced a manpower shortage due to desertions and its own efforts to purge non-Serbs from its ranks. To fill the gaps, its leadership turned to the accused. As he testified in the Milosevic trial, several high-ranking JNA officers visited SRS headquarters to meet with him and discussed sending Seseljevci to the JNA because the JNA was having great problems mobilising conscripts. The accused agreed. And I refer to Exhibit P31 at pages 242 and 243. Witness Petkovic's evidence describes meetings he, as the chief of the war staff, had with Generals Domazetovic and Panic. Petkovic describes one incident in the summer or fall of 1991, in which he, on the accused's behalf, told Generals Domazetovic and Panic that the accused would stop sending volunteers to Croatia unless weapons and uniforms were provided to them more rapidly, which shows the accused's control over the forces he was sending in to the JNA. The generals responded that they could not distribute weapons within Serbia, but weapons would be provided as soon as the Seseljevci left Serbia. The accused accepted this arrangement because he understood that Serbia was not officially involved in the conflict in Croatia. War Staff member Witness Stefanovic also confirmed SRS co-operation with the JNA General Staff and the provision of uniforms and weapons to Seseljevci at JNA barracks. This is found in Exhibit P634 at paragraph 21. Thanks to the accused's agreement with the JNA, thousands of Seseljevci were trained and equipped at JNA barracks in Belgrade and Novi Sad, as seen in Exhibits P857, paragraphs 38 to 41; in P30; in Witness Rankic's evidence in Exhibit P074 [sic] at paragraph 96; in Witness Stojanovic's evidence in Exhibit P528 at paragraph 10; as well as in Exhibit P54 at page 2. Now, the accused has in his brief denied that he co-operated with Milosevic and that he could not possibly have been a JCE member. He had provided no evidentiary support for these propositions. And let us now look at how the accused himself before he was indicted explained how he actually co-operated with Milosevic and a number of other JCE members who we have already heard about today. This is from a video, which has Exhibit number P644, that we have been referring to a number of times. Let's hear the accused.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "This was all done with Milosevic's knowledge, there is no doubt about that, and key people in the police with whom we co-operated at the time where Radmilo Bogdanovic, Mihalj Kertes and others ... Franko Simatovic, also known as Frenki, who later commanded the Red Berets. From the General Staff who mostly co-operated with General Domazetovic who was the deputy Chief of the General Staff and also at the time the head of the personnel administration, if I remember correctly. There were also contacts with lower-ranking officers and so on, depending on the need and the situation. Our volunteers came to Belgrade, the barracks in Bubanj Potok. That is where we put on uniforms and where they were given weapons and buses to take them where they wanted. They were under the command of the JNA as soon as the JNA became involved in the fighting."

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is clear from the evidence that I have discussed so far that the accused co-operated closely with other JCE members to establish Serb fighting forces that could be deployed to create a Serb state. In June 1991, the JNA engaged in an offensive in Croatia. During its operations, it had overall command over Serb Territorial Defence and police forces in Croatia, units of the Serbian MUP, and - as we have seen - Seseljevci that the accused had willingly provided. In his final trial brief, the accused tries to minimise the contribution that he made to the campaign in Croatia by claiming that he was a mere recruitment sergeant for the JNA and that all he did was legal. This is incorrect. Even if the accused's acts had been lawful, legal acts can constitute a significant contribution to a JCE. For this I refer, for example, to the Krajisnik appeals judgement at paragraph 215. Moreover, the accused was not a recruiting sergeant for a legitimate war. He was a fanatic propagandist contributing to an illegal enterprise. He and his fellow JCE members aimed at achieving their nationalistic goals through whatever means necessary - in particular, through the commission of crime. Those crimes began in August 1991 with the persecutorial campaign carried out by Serb forces against the non-Serb population in Croatia. As this Chamber has heard, the crimes committed during Serb forces' campaign in Croatia were inseparable from the campaign itself. JCE member Babic testified in the Milosevic trial that during the war in Croatia, the JNA engaged in combat operations in such a way that it forced not just Croatian armed forces but the entire non-Serb population to withdraw. Even villages that posed no threat to the JNA were completely destroyed. And I refer Your Honours to Exhibit P1137, at pages 92 and 93. At paragraph 92 -- no, sorry, at page 92, Babic testified: "In this way, the JNA, as of August 1991, engaged in a war so that the territories that it captured would be left without any Croatian inhabitants or very few of them. Houses and buildings were destroyed in combat operations and subsequently. Property was looted." The observers of the European Monitoring Mission that were in Croatia at the time described the brutal tactics used by the JNA. The JNA would first terrorise towns into surrendering with heavy artillery fire. Next, undisciplined irregulars - armed and backed by the JNA - would move in on foot and occupy the place. Finally, the JNA would assume overall control. These tactics were not only used against bigger towns like Vukovar, as we will hear, but: "Throughout broad areas of territory in innumerable smaller villages Croatian inhabitants are killed or forced to leave after ... their villages are bulldozed out of existence ... they are simply and wantonly destroyed." That is from Exhibit P412, at page 16. The devastating consequences of this campaign are set out in the Prosecution's closing brief at paragraphs 108 to 116. Here I will just refer Your Honours to Exhibit P632, at pages 76 to 80, which shows that over 200.000 Croatian civilians were expelled from their homes. And not only did the accused send thousands of Seseljevci to participate in this brutal persecutorial campaign. His Seseljevci committed numerous crimes and quickly became so notorious for their brutality and crimes that they were known to international organisations. Helsinki Watch reported in an open letter to Milosevic and other Serbian leaders - that is found in the record as Exhibit P183 - it reported that: "The Serbian government has ... in some cases, supported the formation of at least three paramilitary groups in Serbia which operate in Croatia. What appears to be the most brutal of these groups is led by Vojislav Seselj, the leader of the Serbian Radical Party ... and the Serbian Chetnik Movement." And that is at page 2 of the exhibit. Indeed, the evidence in this case has proven that the accused's Seseljevci committed many crimes charged in the indictment. Your Honours, the evidence that I have discussed and much more evidence discussed in the Prosecution's closing brief proves the criminal nature of the JCE members' common purpose beyond a reasonable doubt. At least by August 1991, the common purpose to pursue a Greater Serbia, to use the accused's terminology, included persecutorial campaign against non-Serbs and the commission of the crimes charged in the indictment. As we will now see, the JCE members soon extended their persecutorial campaign to Bosnia and Herzegovina. While the persecutorial campaign in Croatia was still at its height -- I don't know if Your Honours are wondering whether we should take a break. We could take a break here as we are moving to another area or I can continue until we hit the one hour and a half mark. It's at your disposal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's probably better to have a break. You can then address this other subject. We shall have our traditional 20-minute break. Mr. Seselj, in the event that you do not feel well, we can make a break or have a break when you so wish. Otherwise, we sit for an hour and a half and then have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I expect Mr. Marcussen will feel unwell before I do. Why do you think I would always feel unwell? You could feel unwell too, by the way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. We shall have a 20-minute break and resume in 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall resume the hearing. I had forgotten to mention that since other Judges are sitting in other hearings, we shall resume in this courtroom tomorrow morning at 9.00. And on Wednesday we shall be sitting in the afternoon. So tomorrow morning we start at 9.00 and we had advised all and everyone about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Your Honours, the evidence I discussed before the break proved that the JCE members prepared and deployed Serb forces including Seseljevci in a persecutorial campaign in Croatia as of August 1991. While this persecutorial campaign in Croatia was at its highest, Bosnia and Herzegovina was set on a path to independence. The accused worked with Bosnian Serb leaders, including JCE member Karadzic, to prepare Serb military and political structures to prevent independence. The accused himself sent Seseljevci units to Bosnia and Herzegovina and SRS branches were set up throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is set forth in paragraphs 201 to 207 of the Prosecution's closing brief. On the 15th of October, 1991, the ethnically mixed Assembly of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina debated whether to declare independence. During the debate Radovan Karadzic warned that if the Muslims and Croats were to pursue independence, it would be the same highway of hell as in Croatia. As we will now see, he threatened that the highway would lead as far as to the extinction of the Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Please understand, take it seriously. It is not good what you are doing. This is not the road that you want Bosnia and Herzegovina to take, the same highway to hell and suffering that Slovenia and Croatia went through. Don't think you won't take Bosnia and Herzegovina to hell and Muslim people into possible extinction. Because Muslim people will not be able to defend itself if it comes to war here."

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: This is a clip from Exhibit P1004 and the part that was played is found, if Your Honours want to look at the text, at page 3 of the transcript of that video which is in evidence. Nine days later, the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina nevertheless voted in favour of independence. In response, as they had done in Croatia, the JCE members formed parallel Serb institutions and prepared for war. The accused and other Serb leaders used their experience from Croatia to prepare for war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. As in Croatia, the Bosnian Serb leadership established political and administrative structures. They also created police and Territorial Defence forces. As in Croatia, the accused sent Seseljevci to assist. As in Croatia, Milosevic provided significant support through the JNA and the Serbian MUP. Immediately after the Bosnian Assembly voted for independence, the Bosnian Serb leaders, including Karadzic, Krajisnik, and Plavsic, proclaimed a separate Serb Assembly. Exhibit P931 and AF-1 number 63. Soon thereafter, Karadzic ordered Serb leaders in Bosnian Krajina to establish control in the area, form military units, and subordinate those units to the JNA. The order was fully accepted by local Serb leaders. This is found in the Chamber's adjudicated fact decision from the 23rd of July, 2010, facts numbers 30 and 31. In the Variant A and B instructions from the 19th of December, 1991, the SDS leadership in Bosnia and Herzegovina established Serb-only institutions, like Crisis Staffs, Municipal Assemblies, TO, and police forces. Once formed, the Crisis Staffs were intended to take control of the municipalities. This is in AF-1, number 100, and Exhibits P871 and P957. In this way, Karadzic through the Crisis Staffs exercised control over civilian administrative authorities as well as the Serb military forces in the area, including Serb TOs and police forces. As the Bosnian Serb leadership formalised its plan to take control of targeted areas in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the accused co-operated with his JCE partners. Together, they supported the Bosnian Serb forces and implemented their common purpose in Bosnia and Herzegovina, just as they had done in Croatia. The accused had already in May 1991 established an SRS organisation in Romanija and organised a Chetnik command. This is shown in Exhibits P1162 and 1177. Vojvodas Gavrilovic and Aleksic then organised the SRS in the Romanija region, in co-operation with SRS headquarters in Belgrade. The accused also met his Chetnik commanders in Eastern Herzegovina and in Bosnian Krajina in May 1991, as he stated himself in Exhibit P163. The accused deployed thousands of Seseljevci to Bosnia and Herzegovina, as he said in Exhibits P344 and P347. Many were redeployed fighters from Croatia. As in Croatia, other Serb leaders looked to the accused to support their forces. The accused deployed his Seseljevci at the request of JCE members. For example, the accused deployed Seseljevci to Bosnia and Herzegovina at the request of JCE member Slobodan Milosevic, Exhibit P90, page 6; and JCE member Plavsic sent requests for assistance to the accused and other paramilitary leaders, including Arkan. That is in Exhibit P987. As in Croatia, the accused sent his Seseljevci to crime-base areas and to pattern municipalities in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the request of local Serb leaders. For example, the Serb authorities in Zvornik sent the SRS a request for Seseljevci. In response, the accused sent Witness Rankic and other SRS officials to negotiate with the local authorities and then personally decided to deploy Seseljevci to fight as part of the Zvornik TO. This evidence is in Rankic's statement, which is in evidence as Exhibit P1074 at paragraph 41. Eastern Herzegovina SDS leader Bozidar Vucurevic made a dramatic appeal for Seseljevci to be deployed to his region. The accused then gave a press conference in Trebinje, announcing that he would send volunteers. He subsequently deployed large numbers of Seseljevci to the region. This can be seen in Exhibits P55 and P1109. And Stevan Todorovic, the chief of police in Bosanski Samac, requested Seseljevci from the SRS War Staff. In response, the SRS War Staff redeployed Seseljevci under Vojvoda Srecko Radovanovic, also known as Debeli, from Western Slavonia to Bosanski Samac and placed them under the command of the Bosanski Samac TO. Ljubisa Petkovic, the chief of the accused's War Staff, discussed this deployment in Exhibit C18 at paragraph 49. As in Croatia, the accused remained actively involved with his Seseljevci. He and members of his War Staff co-operated with other JCE members to ensure that his Seseljevci were armed, trained, and equipped. By February 1992, the accused and his Seseljevci were ready for war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. After asserting that the Serbian people would never allow Bosnia and Herzegovina to be independent or a sovereign state, he announced: "We are ready for war ... our Serbian Radical Party and the ... Chetnik Movement act in all areas of Bosnia and Herzegovina." This is in Exhibit P1192, pages 1 and 2. As they had done in Croatia, Milosevic and the JNA leadership also gave support to the Bosnian Serb leadership. They redeployed significant forces and equipment from Croatia to Bosnia and Herzegovina. Expert Theunens explained at transcript pages 4024 to 4026 how this worked. For instance, the JNA redeployed an armoured brigade to the area of Zvornik, which later participated in the attack on Zvornik. Also, on the 5th of December, 1991, Milosevic and Kadijevic agreed to reorganise the JNA so that when the JNA would be forced to leave Bosnia and Herzegovina, it could leave behind men and equipment under Karadzic's authority. This plan was implemented in May 1992, when the VRS was created. I refer Your Honours to Exhibit P198, page 10; and AF-1, fact numbers 186, 190, and 191. Milosevic also provided assistance to the Bosnian Serb leadership through the Serbian MUP. The Serbian MUP trained and supplied both Seseljevci and local Serbs. Hundreds of Seseljevci were trained at MUP centres pursuant to an agreement between the accused himself and the MUP. Witness Petkovic explains this in, for example, Exhibit C16, paragraph 48. And the Serbian MUP's Red Berets, whose training camps were already mentioned, deployed their special police force to Bosnia. And involved, for example, in Bosanski Samac and Nevesinje. This can be seen in Exhibit P131 at page 6. As my colleagues will be discussing, the JNA, the Serbian MUP, and the SDS arranged considerable arming of civilians and so-called volunteers. At this juncture I will just mention Exhibit P257, page 6. It is a JNA report from March 1992, and it shows the presence of almost 70.000 "volunteers" in the 2nd Military District who had been armed by the JNA or by the SDS. By the end of March 1992, the JCE members were ready for war. Krajisnik told the Serbian Assembly in Bosnia and Herzegovina: "... it would be good if we could start implementing what we have agreed upon - the ethnic division on the ground." That is from Exhibit P951, page 12. And on the 24th of March, 1992, Krajisnik told the Serb Assembly that at the appropriate time: "... all the Serbian municipalities, both the old ones and the newly established ones, would literally assume control of the entire territory of the municipality concerned." That is from Exhibit P952, page 22. Soon afterwards, Serb forces began to carve out Serb-claimed areas from Bosnia and Herzegovina. Serb forces composed of the JNA and later the VRS, local Serbian TO and police units, Serbian MUP units, Arkan's men, and Seseljevci carried out a massive persecutorial campaign against the non-Serb civilian population in Bosnia and Herzegovina. As in Croatia, the results of this persecutorial campaign were devastating. Your Honours now have on your monitors Exhibit P669. This map shows the demographic composition of Bosnia and Herzegovina right before the war in 1991. The red and light-red areas were areas with a significant Serb population. Green areas were majority Muslim areas. Blue areas were majority Croat. And purple and grey areas are mixed populations. As Your Honours can see, it is a fairly complex patchwork. We'll now look at how the situation looked after the persecutorial campaign. Now on your monitors you have Exhibit P629. It shows the ethnic composition in 1997. The colours are still the same. Red areas are Serb areas, green areas are Muslim areas, and blue areas are Croat areas. And as can be simply seen, the geographic composition of Bosnia and Herzegovina had been completely changed. The crimes in Zvornik, Greater Sarajevo, Mostar, and Nevesinje that have been proven in this case were beyond a reasonable doubt part of this campaign. In conclusion, Your Honours, the evidence proves that the accused co-operated closely with other JCE members to pursue their common goal of a Serb state. They set up Serb-only institutions. They established police and military forces. When first Croatia and later Bosnia and Herzegovina declared independence, they deployed these forces in areas that they claimed as Serb land. At least from August 1991, these forces waged a massive persecutorial campaign against non-Serbs in the targeted areas. The crimes in Vukovar, Zvornik, Greater Sarajevo, Mostar, and Nevesinje were part of this persecutorial campaign. The crimes were committed by the accused's Seseljevci and other Serb forces commanded or controlled by other JCE members. The accused himself described the result of this campaign and his co-operation with Milosevic. He said: "The result of our co-operation and joint efforts was the creation of Republika Srpska and the Republic of Serbian Krajina. Without our support and that of the Socialist Party of Serbia, I do not believe that the Serbs of Republika Srpska and the Republic of the Serbian Krajina would have succeeded in their struggle to attain their own countries." That is from Exhibit P1249 at page 2. Your Honours, the evidence proves beyond a reasonable doubt that there existed a common purpose of which the accused was a part to commit the crimes charged in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Before handing over to Ms. Biersay, I will address some evidentiary issues. As Your Honours have seen, the accused made numerous admissions before the indictment period that have proved his membership in and contribution to the JCE. The accused has subsequently denied some of these prior admissions. The sworn and unsworn statements made by the accused after his indictment requires careful scrutiny. The accused's self-serving denials should be rejected when they are without corroboration of other significant, independent, and credible evidence, because he has a motive to shape his statements to evade criminal responsibility. Other witnesses, either closely connected to the accused or listed in his Defence final trial brief as Defence witnesses, have recanted their prior statements which inculpate the accused or simply have not appeared to testify. The statements of these witnesses were admitted into evidence and are reliable. The reliability of these statements is verified by admitted suspect interviews as well as by the testimony of a member of the Office of the Prosecutor, the OTP, and by other reliable, corroborative evidence. Some of the recanting witnesses made outlandish allegations against OTP staff during their testimony in an effort to discredit their prior written statements to the OTP. The accused has repeated these claims in his final trial brief. However, an independent Court-appointed inquiry conducted a comprehensive review of these allegations. The allegations were rejected. The Trial Chamber accepted the conclusions of the inquiry. These recantations are not worthy of credit. The recantations were the product of an organised campaign to deter witnesses from testifying truthfully. The Trial Chamber should reject all the accused's arguments that he rely on witnesses' incredible recantations or challenges -- I'm sorry, Your Honours. I will start that over again. The Trial Chamber should reject all of the accused's arguments that rely on witnesses' incredible recantations or that challenges the admitted statements of non-appearing witnesses. I refer Your Honours to the argumentative appendix to the Prosecution's closing brief which addresses these issues in greater detail. That, Your Honours, concludes my submissions for now. Ms. Biersay will present the Prosecution's arguments regarding the accused's contribution to the common purpose that I have just discussed, and we will have to re-arrange the Prosecution here for a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good evening, Ms. Biersay. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Before I begin my presentation, I wanted to just verify the timing of the next break so I could be consistent with the Court's schedule. By my calculation, if we do the hour and a half, we'd be -- it would be 6.40. So I'm not sure if you would want to take a break at 6.40 or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd rather we went non-stop until the end, but if Mr. Seselj is tired he will tell us.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you for the clarification. Thank you, Your Honours. Your Honours, the accused poisoned and pounded non-Serbs and Serbs with his campaign of hatred throughout the former Yugoslavia. He did so as a deputy of the National Assembly of the Republic of Serbia. He did so as the leader of the Serbian Radical Party, the second-most popular party in Serbia. He did so as the quasi-military leader known throughout the former Yugoslavia by his military Chetnik title: Vojvoda. And he did so as the charismatic media star who advocated the forcible creation of Greater Serbia. The power and authority implicit in his political and military trappings made it crystal clear to non-Serbs as well as to Serbs that the words he wielded as weapons should be taken seriously. Serbs and non-Serbs saw for themselves that the accused could and did make his threats of violence real, he did it through sympathisers and he did it through his Seseljevci. In his brief and throughout this trial, the accused has tried to persuade the Chamber that during the indictment period he was a simple opposition politician and that he is now being prosecuted merely for his political ideology. As a matter of fact, as a matter of law, his being a politician does not absolve him of his responsibility for committing, aiding and abetting, and instigating the charged crimes. And this is discussed in detail in the Prosecution's closing brief at paragraphs 96 to 107, paragraphs 247 to 274, and paragraphs 566 to 609. Your Honours, in this segment of the presentation, I will highlight some key points relating to three general areas: One, the accused's influence and authority during the indictment period; two, his contribution to the common purpose and to the charged crimes through his hate propaganda against non-Serbs; and three, his contribution to the common purpose and to the charged crimes through his recruitment and deployment of volunteers. The accused significantly contributed to the implementation of the common criminal purpose and he substantially contributed to the commission of crimes, and he did so through his two contributions, the hate propaganda and his campaign to recruit, deploy, and encourage volunteers. His contribution to these crimes also shows his intent to commit them. For his hate speeches in Vukovar and Hrtkovci he is guilty of physically committing persecution and other crimes. Throughout the indictment period, this accused held political, quasi-military, and popular influence and authority. He exploited that influence and authority, first, to aggravate inter-ethnic tensions and brutally attack non-Serbs in order to drive them out of targeted areas; and to recruit, deploy, and encourage those willing to forcibly and criminally further his goal of creating Greater Serbia. The accused seized the disintegration of Yugoslavia to inspire fear and incite discriminatory crimes. And that's why JCE members requested and encouraged his contributions. Reliable and credible evidence proves beyond a reasonable doubt in this case that the accused fully intended the resulting criminal campaign of persecution in Croatia, in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Hrtkovci in Serbia. Was the accused a politician during the indictment period? Absolutely. And a very successful one. During the conflict in Croatia and BiH, the accused - leader of the SRS and a National Assembly deputy - was the charismatic public face of an ultra-nationalist policy that promoted a homogeneous Greater Serbia. Its western borders, as you have heard, ran along the infamous KOKV: Karlobag-Ogulin-Karlovac-Virovitica line. Exhibits P156, P157, and P158, and the tables V, VI, and VIII in those exhibits, and those are the election results from May and December of 1992. According to those exhibits, the SRS was the second-most popular party after the SPS. This was true for both the Federal Assembly and the National Assembly of Serbia. Now, in 1993, the accused admitted that during the indictment period the public perception was that the accused and the SRS held extensive political influence, partly because of their co-operation with Milosevic and the SPS. And that co-operation was in assisting Serbs outside of Serbia. As the accused himself put it: "... many people had the impression that we Radicals were in coalition with Socialists." And he admitted this in his own periodical "Zapadna Srbija," which is admitted as Exhibit P1230. In August 1993, the accused conceded - in Exhibit P1224 - that he contributed to the power of Milosevic because Milosevic had "the backing of the second most powerful party, the Serbian Radical Party." The accused went on to describe his significant political influence, saying: "I do not have any state functions, but I have a greater authority than some ministers. And you can object all you want, but authority is authority and cannot be measured through titles but through realistic political strength." The evidence has shown how the accused abused his political strength. The core purpose of the SRS was not merely to engage in politics but to forcibly impose a Serb-dominated state, cleansed of non-Serbs. In Exhibit P1183, the accused participated in a televised interview during the height of war in Croatia in November 1991. He distinguished the SRS from other political parties because of its contributions to the war - the SRS, in his words, "was not a party which holds more press conferences rather than firing bullets on the front." Your Honours, this accused was more than a simple politician. He was a politician who held the highest Chetnik military title: Vojvoda. This deferential title was recognised by many, including volunteers. He headed the Serbian Chetnik Movement, an unregistered movement grafted onto the registered SRS to become its Chetnik military wing. And as has been shown, he wore military garb and was often escorted by armed, uniformed men. The accused has cultivated this belligerent, militaristic, personal, and organisational identity, and he did that even before becoming a deputy and before creating the SRS. Deliberately evoking the powerful ideology and symbols of the Chetnik Movement, the accused became its most prominent representative. He described, for example, the impact of an important symbol of the Chetnik Movement, the Chetnik flag, and he described the impact of that flag on non-Serbs. And this is what he said: "Firstly, black flags are the main hallmark of the Chetnik Movement ... they are very effective; you know when those Chetnik units with black flags show up in places where there are Ustashas, Ustashas run for their lives. Where 50 Chetniks show up, Croats think there are 10.000 of them and they flee in panic." Exhibit P1181. The framing of the combined SRS/SCP as a military force was complete by the time the accused commanded his Seseljevci and contributed them to Serb forces to implement the common criminal purpose. He described himself in Exhibit P217, signed by him in 1993, that he was: "... the only Serbian Chetnik Vojvoda directly involved in the current liberation movement of the Serbian people, and following the tradition of the Serbian Chetniks. I hereby confer the title of Serbian Chetnik Vojvoda upon the following most prominent Chetnik commanders for their remarkable war services, great valour and demonstrated combat skills." And he is talking about the titles that he gave to his Vojvodas. The ceremony conferring the titles of Vojvoda to his fighters in 1993 was attended by many uniformed and armed Seseljevci. It was also publicised, publicised showing the force of the Seseljevci, and this is in Exhibit P255 which I'd like to show to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Reporter 2: On the first day of the referendum, Dr. Vojislav Seselj, the Serbian Chetnik Vojvoda and the president of the Serbian Radical Party, arrived today in Republika Srpska. As soon as he crossed the Drina River, he went to visit our defenders on the first line of defence, afterwards, Knezina, a village and monastery in the free Serbian Romanija, the oath of the new Serbian Chetnik Vojvodas. "Unknown man: Order number 124. As the only Chetnik Vojvoda directly engaged in the present-day" --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a historical and very valuable material, and yet I can't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "... Chetnik commanders, I hereby pronounce ... "Reporter: Romanija, a mountain that doesn't speak to its enemies, rejoiced at the oath of 18 new Vojvodas, an oath it didn't hear for 50 years. "Vojvodas: I swear as the Serbian Chetnik Vojvoda ... "Seselj: I swear to God and Saint Sava ..." Vojvodas: [No interpretation] "Seselj: That I will fight with all my might for the freedom of the Serbian people ... "Vojvodas: That I will fight with all my might for the freedom of the Serbian people ... "Seselj: And the restoration of a unified Serbian state in the Balkans which will encompass all Serbian lands ... "Vojvodas: And the restoration of a unified Serbian state on the Balkans which will encompass all Serbian lands ... "Seselj: So God help me. "Vojvodas: So God help me. "Seselj: Good luck and bless you. May God give you a long life. "Reporter: One can trust them that it is going to be like this. The rank of Chetnik Vojvoda was bestowed on these Serbian heros from all Serbian areas: Zdravko Abramovic; Branislav Vakic; Srecko Radovanovic; Slavko Crnic; Nedeljko Vidikovac; Slavko Aleksic; Mitar Maksimovic, Manda; Miroslav Vukovic, Cele; Milika Dacevic, Ceko; Tomislav Nikolic; Milan Lancuzanin, Kameni; Zoran Drazinovic, Cica; Jovo Ostojic; Ljubisa Petkovic; Todor Lazic; Mirko Blagojevic; Dragan Svetkovic; and Branislav Gavrilovic, Brne. "Brne, Brne, turn around just a little so I can capture you like that."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: The accused is not charged with command responsibility. However, his authority and influence over the politico-military, quasi-military SRS/SCP is relevant to the nature of his contribution to the common purpose as well as his legal responsibility as an aider and abettor and instigator. Senior members of the SRS/SCP, like Witnesses Petkovic, Rankic, and Glamocanin describe the accused as having "absolute power" over the combined SRS/SCP. In their words, the accused was an "autocrat." He was a "dictator." And that, for example, can be found in Exhibit C13, pages 26 to 27. The accused revelled in his authoritarian roles throughout the conflict, describing himself with military-style titles like "commander," "the supreme commander," and as "the commander of the operative detachments of the SCP in the homeland." This is set out in Exhibits P59, P154, and P1058. And he was proud of this authority which he reinforced publicly, saying: "I organise interventions by our guerilla organisation and I define aims of attack and points that have to be won." After the shelling of Vukovar, for example, while non-Serbs were fleeing and before the brutal crimes of Ovcara and Velepromet, the accused held rallies where he was escorted by armed body-guards, uniformed, armed body-guards. The effect was clear, as VS-002 told the Chamber as transcript page 6557: "He was a Vojvoda. We would not have refused his order." The accused's position as the undisputed Chetnik leader and Vojvoda within the SRS/SCP and his perceived legitimacy as a politician all facilitated his indoctrination of the Serb forces, especially to embed fear and hatred, justifying ethnic separation and forcible removal of non-Serbs. That evidence is beyond a reasonable doubt. Also during the indictment period, as described in Exhibit P1182, the accused was a media star. That status amplified his already significant audience for his campaign of hatred against non-Serbs. It also amplified and intensified the quality of his contribution to and encouragement of the charged crimes. In addition to the extensive coverage he received in the media, the accused created his own media machinery to disseminate his propaganda, such as press conferences and his two SRS publications: "Velika Srbija" and "Zapadna Srbija." He also appealed to the public through personal appearances and rallies. His popularity and influence won him yet another title, that of 1991's "Man of the Year," given to him by the media in Serbia as shown in Exhibit P1190. The accused's media coverage facilitated his war on non-Serbs, whereby he used his words as weapons in his persecution campaign. As the accused acknowledged in Exhibit P1337: "Propaganda is based on the fact that the vast majority of people are naturally ready to believe indiscriminately in everything they read, hear, or see on television." Several ground-level perpetrators committed crimes soon after listening to the accused's hate propaganda, like in Vukovar and Hrtkovci. Some cited his ideas as driving them to "clean up" non-Serbs, as in Exhibit P57. He inspired thousands to join the ranks of Seseljevci. This shows that his hate propaganda had a demonstrable impact on the persecution campaign as it unfolded on the ground. The confluence of the accused's political influence, his quasi-military authority, media coverage, and campaign of hatred against non-Serbs was a lethal and criminal mix that furthered the common purpose. Witness Oberschall defined propaganda as: "... a technique of persuasion that is based on emotional appeals." He explained that threats - and other propaganda tools - operate to create a "demand for action." And this is at transcript page 2054. He also described repetition as being a key component to successful propaganda. Repeated and repeated and repeated hateful propaganda imbues its audience with hate, even turning some to violence to remove a perceived threat - that threat, according to this accused, was non-Serbs. Before and during the indictment period, the accused was relentless in his promotion of a Greater Serbia; relentless in his labelling of Croats as "Ustashi"; relentless in his degrading language about Bosniaks; relentless in his advocation of genocidal threats to Serbs; and relentless in his inciting calls for revenge. Together, all a significant contribution to the purpose. Together, all building a coercive environment and conditioning the minds of both non-Serbs and sympathisers. These instigating propaganda contributions - which I will now highlight - came into lethal fruition with the commencement of the charged crimes. The accused espoused Chetnik-based ideology to recruit Serb fighters and to create fear in non-Serbs. He again and again advocated force to gain and retain what he considered Serb lands outside of Serbia. He again and again proclaimed that Serbs, Croats, and Muslims simply could not live together, as in Exhibits P1298 and 1211. He again and again denigrated non-Serbs to promote contempt and hatred for them, and he warned that non-Serbs posed a physical, demographic, cultural, and even economic threat to Serbs, like in Exhibits P1295 and 1280. Again and again and again this accused and his political and quasi-military machinery - the SRS/SCP - evoked past victimisation and genocide against Serbs in order to advocate and justify criminal revenge and violence against non-Serbs; in other words, to justify the crimes necessary to the common purpose. In Exhibit P35, for example, he threatened: "All those with an unclear conscience should fear us Serbs. They have reason to fear us. We Serbs have forgotten and forgiven too much in history. We have told the Croats should they ever again resort to genocidal activities against the Serbian people, not only shall we take revenge for every victim, but we shall also settle scores for the victims from World War I and World War II." Public declarations of this kind were designed to encourage Serbs to perpetrate crimes against non-Serbs and to absolve them of responsibility for committing such crimes. The accused himself has admitted in Exhibit P1215 that "words can be a very dangerous weapon. Sometimes they pound like a howitzer." As he now faces criminal charges, he wants you to believe that words, his words, had no power at all. The evidence shows that to be false. He knew his hate propaganda pounded like a howitzer. The evidence has proven him to be right. He pounded non-Serbs in Croatia with his hateful words. He pounded non-Serbs in BiH. And he pounded non-Serbs in Hrtkovci. When he called for Greater Serbia, he was promoting and justifying the subjugation, expulsion, and maltreatment of non-Serbs. As inter-ethnic tensions increased and erupted, his words continued to pound non-Serbs. I would now highlight some of the accused's pounding hate propaganda directed at Croats in Croatia. According to the accused himself, he was invited to Plitvice in April of 1991, shortly before the indictment period, and he was invited by Milan Babic, member of the Serb leadership of the new SAO Krajina. In Plitvice around this time there already had been a recent killing of two policemen, a Croat and a Serb. The accused chose that occasion to deliver an inflammatory speech to a large Serb audience. He warned them that they would be sold and promised them: "... we will avenge Serb blood." The Trial Chamber can observe in Exhibit P339 the impact of the accused's speech on the crowd. Now I ask that that be played at this time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Journalist: In such an atmosphere Vojvoda Seselj, announced already at the beginning of the meeting, started his speech. "Seselj: Serbian people live here, this is Serbian land and it will remain Serbian forever. "Audience: That's right, that's right. "Journalist: After labelling the decision on the establishing of the Serbian Autonomous District of Krajina historical, Seselj said: "Seselj: Serbian brothers and Serbian sisters. You find yourselves in the front lines defending the Serbian cause."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again I can't hear anything. These are the words of a genius that I'm still proud of even today, but I can't hear a thing --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Perhaps someone can assist the accused in handling the volume over his controls.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have increased the volume, but I could not hear anything. You may have noticed that when I addressed you, Your Honours, my volume was at the maximum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... to turn up the volume for us to hear.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Your Honours, we'll ask that the technicians come in at this time, and what I'll do is I will read the intros and we can play the videos back to back once we have the audio at a proper level. In that speech, in Exhibit 339, the accused told his audience: "We're sending a message to the new Ustasha head of state and Ustasha regime in Croatia: Serbian heads have rolled ... a Serbian head has rolled in Serbian Western Srem and Slavonia ... we will avenge Serbian blood." Soon after that speech, the accused gave another one shortly thereafter, on the 21st of April, 1991, in Jagodniak, Croatia, in Baranja, where Serbs had faced brutal crimes in World War II. There, the accused evoked the genocide of Serbs and declared that Croats could only have land west of the KOKV line. In Exhibit P70, when it's played, the Chamber will see -- will hear and see that the applause was most enthusiastic when the accused repeated his infamous refrain about the Karlobag-Ogulin-Karlovac-Virovitica line.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Croats, as far as we are concerned, you can leave Yugoslavia if you want to. Whenever they want to, they can leave, but we are openly letting them know that they will not take away a square foot of Serb territory, not one piece of land where there are Serbian villages, destroyed churches, Serbian mass graves, Serbian camps, the Serbian Jasenovac. If we allowed that, we would be unworthy of our glorious ancestors and we would have to be ashamed before our descendents. The Croats can create their new state but only west of the Karlobag-Ogulin-Karlovac-Virovitica line. Everything -- everything east of that line is Serbian."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And that was Exhibit 70. And at this time we will try again to play Exhibit P339.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Journalist: In such an atmosphere, Vojvoda Seselj, announced already at the beginning of the meeting, started his speech. "Crowds shouting: Vojo! Vojo! Serbia! Serbia! "Seselj: This is Serbian land. Here Serbian people live, and it will remain Serbian forever. "Audience: That's right! That's right! "Journalist: After labelling the decision on the establishment of the Serbian Autonomous District of Krajina historic, Seselj said: "Seselj: Serbian brothers and Serbian sisters, you find yourselves in the front lines defending the Serb cause. Serbian state borders. You are in the most difficult position and you are the pride of the whole of Serbdom. "Journalist: He has promised them that they would not be left to themselves and that all the Serbs in Croatia have only one party, the Serbian Democratic Party. "Seselj: You have a wise and brave leadership here, headed by the heroic Dr. Milan Babic. "Journalist: Those who divide the Serbian people he labelled as traitors. "Seselj: Only Ante Markovic's mercenaries and those of foreign intelligence services believe today that there are more important problems than your defence, your protection. They are offering you up to Tudjman. They would sell you. You will not be sold or betrayed. "Journalist: Instead of calming them down, Seselj sent a message to the gathered people at the end. "Seselj: We are sending a message to the new Ustasha head of state and the Ustasha regime in Croatia: Serbian heads have rolled, struck down by the Ustasha hand in the Serbian Krajina. A Serbian head has rolled and we will avenge it."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: In the same month that he gave those speeches, he deployed Seseljevci to Borovo Selo. After his volunteer deployment, after his speeches there, Seseljevci participated in ambushing and killing Croat police in Borovo Selo on the 2nd of May, 1991. The accused was unrelenting. At an Orthodox celebration attended by Karadzic, four days later on the 6th of May, 1991, the accused warned the Serb crowd about a new genocide against the Serb people, about avenging those crimes, and about Chetniks fighting throughout Croatia. And this is captured in Exhibit P353, which I'll ask be played now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Our western enemies are attempting to carry out a new genocide against the Serbian people. Brothers and sister Serbs, it is our duty to stop it and we are sending this message to our enemies: Not only shall we avenge the present victims, but we shall avenge the previous ones too, when they dared to put the Ustasha knife under the Serbian throat again. "Bosnia and the brave Serbian Herzegovina people, it is particularly you who must not allow to be divided. You have one political party, the Serbian Democratic Party, you have your leadership which has proven its qualities in action, on the front lines, and which has upheld the honour of Serbdom.
